newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao briefly arrested, released on bail.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao briefly arrested, released on bail.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was briefly arrested at his home on criminal forgery charges and then immediately freed on bail, authorities said on Thursday.

Rao's arrest and release late on Wednesday marked the latest chapter in a tangled legal saga which has forced the former prime minister to step down as Congress party leader and shaken the balance of power between his party and the government.

An official with the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said two federal police officers served an arrest warrant on Rao at his heavily guarded New Delhi residence on Wednesday at around 8.45 p.m. (1515 GMT).
Rao immediately provided 50,000 rupees ($1,400) in bail and was released. The CBI officers left 30 minutes after arriving, the official said, adding: "It was a technical arrest".
The arrest warrant was issued last week by a New Delhi judge but had been temporarily suspended pending a ruling by the Delhi High Court on a plea by Rao for legal protection against arrest.
Rao's forgery case dates from 1989. Last month, federal police charged the former prime minister and five others with using false documents to defame a rival politician.

On Wednesday, the High Court granted Rao the right to pay pre-emptive, or anticipatory, bail which would last until a hearing into the forgery case, which is set for next Monday. Rao has not commented publicly on the charges.
He has been ordered to appear at next Monday's hearing, where he could request ordinary bail. If bail is denied, he would be taken into custody pending completion of the trial.
Rao stepped down as Congress leader last month after a judge upheld a summons ordering the politician to appear in court in a separate case of criminal conspiracy to cheat.
Rao says he is innocent of accusations he helped cheat a businessman of $100,000 in 1983. A hearing in the cheating case has been scheduled for October 16.
In addition to the forgery and cheating cases, Rao has been linked to a vote-buying scandal.
Lawmakers of the regional Jharkand Mukti Morcha party say they were paid $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion which Rao's Congress-led government survived by a razor-thin margin.
Earlier this year, the CBI filed a case accusing Rao and other Congress leaders of buying the votes. They have denied any wrongdoing. The case is still under investigation.
Rao's troubles have undermined his authority within India's oldest party and triggered a leadership struggle.

Fallout from his legal cases extends well beyond the party as Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition depends on Congress to survive a parliamentary challenge by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Congress's new leader, Sitaram Kesri, has threatened to withdraw support for Deve Gowda's centre-left United Front coalition unless it offers reciprocal support for Congress and its low-caste ally in the populous Uttar Pradesh state, which recently held local elections. Vote counting was underway on Thursday.

Kesri's threat has stirred worries among foreign investors that a period of political uncertainty has set in. That, they fear, could jeopardise the economic reform programme which Rao launched in 1991 but which foreign firms argue needs to be pushed forward to guarantee strong economic growth in India.
